name: Zephaniah
role: Prophet of the Day of the LORD under Josiah
whenBasis: In the days of Josiah (Zephaniah 1:1), whom Thiele dates 640–609 BC.
summary: Son of Cushi, whose descent is traced four generations back to a Hezekiah, prophesying in the days of Josiah. He announced the great Day of the LORD, near and coming quickly, a day of wrath against Judah's worship of Baal and the host of heaven and against the nations around. It ends in joy: the LORD in Jerusalem's midst will rejoice over her with singing.
body: He condemns those who bow on the rooftops to the stars and swear by Milcom, and the complacent who say the LORD will do nothing, good or bad. A meek and humble people will be left, who trust in the name of the LORD.

moments.text: Against Baal and the host of heaven

later.text: The medieval hymn Dies irae takes its opening from Zephaniah 1:15 in the Latin Vulgate, “dies irae dies illa.”

sources.title: Dies irae, sequence of the Latin Requiem Mass

later.text: The last of his forebears, Hezekiah, is spelled as the king's name, though the text does not call him king. Ibn Ezra takes him to be King Hezekiah, the line being traced back to its most honoured member, and Amariah a brother of Manasseh; Radak reports the reading as possible but unproven. A. R. Fausset answers that the absence of “king of Judah” is fatal to it.

sources.title: Ibn Ezra on Zephaniah 1:1
sources.note: Hebrew: 'הזכיר הכתוב שמות האבות עד שהגיע לנכבד והוא חזקיהו המלך' (rendered here: scripture names the forebears until it reaches the honoured one, King Hezekiah); Gill reports the reading as Aben Ezra's

sources.title: Radak on Zephaniah 1:1
sources.note: Hebrew: 'י"א כי חזקיה זה חזקיה מלך יהודה ואפשר אלא שאין בזה ראיה' (rendered here: some say this Hezekiah is Hezekiah king of Judah, and it is possible, but there is no proof of it)

sources.title: Commentary Critical and Explanatory on the Whole Bible, introduction to Zephaniah
sources.author: A. R. Fausset
sources.note: 'Yet the omission of the designation, "king of Judah," is fatal to the theory'

traditions: not the king: A. R. Fausset
